summary.text: One **axis** (hypothalamus → pituitary → gland) with **negative feedback**: every exogenous hormone suppresses the levels above it.

**Acromegaly**: octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant (monitor IGF-1); **prolactinoma**: cabergoline; **DI**: desmopressin (hyponatremia); **SIADH**: fluid restriction, then tolvaptan (start in hospital).

chunks.text: **One regulatory template governs thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal control alike.**

**Figure 1. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the hypothalamus drives the anterior pituitary, which drives a target endocrine gland, whose peripheral hormone produces end-organ effects and negatively feeds back to suppress the levels above it.**
This is the conceptual spine for the unit — thyroid, adrenal and gonadal pharmacology all map onto this three-level axis; return to it every time a new gland appears.
The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — which explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit suppresses the levels above it.
Somatropin (GH deficiency); octreotide, lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH excess); cabergoline, bromocriptine (prolactin); desmopressin (DI); tolvaptan, demeclocycline (SIADH).
GH axis (Figure 2): pituitary somatotroph releases GH → GH drives liver IGF-1 production → octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release.
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls → acromegaly symptoms improve (monitor IGF-1). GH rises on pegvisomant, so GH is not used to monitor it.

Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release — dopamine agonists restore that inhibitory tone. Hypothalamic dopamine is the brake on lactotrophs; prolactinoma or drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) lift the brake.
Cabergoline or bromocriptine activate D2 receptors → prolactin release falls and the tumor often shrinks → cycles and fertility return; galactorrhea resolves.
ADH (Figure 4): ADH binds the V2 receptor in the collecting duct → aquaporin-2 channels insert → water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
Desmopressin boosts this (diabetes insipidus); tolvaptan or demeclocycline blunt it (SIADH) → free water retained in DI therapy, excreted in SIADH therapy.
Anterior pituitary hormones & their hypothalamic regulators: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs down-regulate GnRH receptors and suppress LH and FSH.
**●  GH deficiency:** treated with recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin); monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 levels in adults.

**●  GH excess (acromegaly):** treated with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide — suppress GH release), the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or dopamine agonists (cabergoline) in select cases.
**●  Clinical pearl:** octreotide also has major uses outside the pituitary axis — variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome — worth flagging as a cross-system agent.
**●  Indication:** octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly; octreotide also treats carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.
Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine agonists are first-line — cabergoline, bromocriptine — used for prolactinomas and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency/resistance): desmopressin (DDAVP) for central DI. SIADH (ADH excess): fluid restriction first-line; vasopressin-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline for refractory cases.
**●  Somatropin (GH deficiency):** monitor growth velocity or IGF-1.
**●  Adverse effects:** GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia with octreotide and lanreotide (also glucose changes).
**●  Limitation:** pegvisomant does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.
**●  Adverse effects:** nausea, orthostatic hypotension and dizziness (dopamine agonists).
Cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated; high doses link to valvulopathy.
**●  Caution:** high-dose cabergoline in Parkinson patients is linked to cardiac valve fibrosis; use caution with severe psychiatric disease and avoid unmonitored antipsychotic changes.
**●  Desmopressin:** risk is hyponatremia; monitor sodium and limit fluids.
**●  Tolvaptan:** can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and cause liver injury; start in hospital.
**●  SIADH:** first-line is fluid restriction; demeclocycline causes photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity.
Short stature from GH deficiency, Turner syndrome and other growth disorders is the main somatropin use; long-acting weekly forms (somapacitan) exist.
Growth hormone (somatropin) adverse effects are rare: pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression, edema, hyperglycemia.
Mecasermin (recombinant IGF-I for GH-unresponsive growth failure) causes hypoglycemia — give with a carbohydrate meal within 20 minutes.
Octreotide: nausea, cramps, steatorrhea, gallstones, and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.
Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin by blocking dopamine.
**●  Dosing:** cabergoline is better tolerated and given twice weekly; bromocriptine is daily.
Octreotide is 45 times more potent than somatostatin at inhibiting GH; somatostatin analogs come as long-acting monthly depots. Cabergoline’s half-life is about 65 hours.
**●  Monitoring:** pregnancy testing and prolactin monitoring (dopamine agonists). Monitor IGF-1 for acromegaly therapy.
Pegvisomant does not lower GH secretion and may let the adenoma grow — monitor IGF-I and yearly pituitary MRI.
DI vs. SIADH is a classic exam pairing — opposite problems; anchor it to "which way does free water move" rather than drug names in isolation.
Octreotide reappears in GI/variceal contexts — drug classes are not siloed by organ system.
Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism — infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in women; low libido and ED in men; macroadenomas can compress the optic nerves.
Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is given IV to start or augment labor; it also triggers milk letdown. Its half-life is about 5 minutes.
Problem · Diabetes insipidus: ADH deficiency/resistance — water lost · SIADH: ADH excess — water retained
Drug · Diabetes insipidus: Desmopressin (central DI) · SIADH: Fluid restriction; tolvaptan or demeclocycline if refractory
Watch for · Diabetes insipidus: Hyponatremia — limit fluids · SIADH: Overcorrection (osmotic demyelination); liver injury; photosensitivity

chunks.text: Why is GH useless for monitoring pegvisomant? The drug blocks the receptor, not the release — GH actually rises; IGF-1 is what falls.
**Replacing a deficient gland, or slowing down an overactive one.**

**Figure 6. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): iodide trapping, organification, and coupling produce T3/T4, which undergo peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling, while PTU additionally blocks peripheral conversion.**
Figure 6 is the key to the next slides: PTU, not methimazole, is preferred in thyroid storm because it blocks an extra step.
Levothyroxine (replacement); methimazole, propylthiouracil (thionamides); propranolol; potassium iodide.
**Mechanism: synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3.**
Levothyroxine path (Figure 5): tablet taken on an empty stomach → absorbed in the small intestine; calcium, iron and antacid binders block it.
T4 converted to active T3 in tissues → T3 binds nuclear receptors and restores metabolism → TSH falls to the target range (recheck at 6–8 weeks).
Methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling; PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion — a faster symptomatic effect in crisis.
Storm targets (Figure 7): Graves thyroid makes excess hormone — PTU blocks synthesis; hormone is released — iodine (after PTU) blocks release.

T4 converts to T3 in tissues — PTU, propranolol and steroids block conversion; T3 stimulates beta receptors — propranolol blunts tachycardia and tremor; crisis settles with fluids, cooling and support.
Thyroid physiology: large doses of iodine inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff block); amiodarone, contrast, β blockers and corticosteroids inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion.
Levothyroxine: first-line for hypothyroidism; narrow therapeutic index — dose titrated using TSH (primary hypothyroidism) with repeat labs every 6–8 weeks after a dose change.
About 1.6 mcg/kg/day is full replacement; estrogen raises needs. **●  Pregnancy:** often raises dose needs; monitor TSH closely.
Methimazole: first-line for most non-pregnant patients — once-daily dosing, more convenient; avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
PTU: preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm. PTU first trimester (lower teratogenic risk) and thyroid storm (also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).
**A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.** Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets.

Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. PTU (preferred over methimazole) — blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.

Iodine solution (given after PTU/methimazole) — acutely blocks hormone release; must follow the antithyroid drug to avoid providing substrate for new synthesis. Corticosteroids — blunt peripheral conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

Laboratory diagnosis of Graves disease: suppressed TSH with high free thyroid hormone. Management of Graves disease: antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy; methimazole preferred except in pregnancy and storm.
Pregnant hypothyroid patients often need about 25–30% more levothyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.
Methimazole boxed warning: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. PTU boxed warning: severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole) — reserve for specific indications.
Thioamide agranulocytosis occurs in 0.1–0.5%, usually within the first 90 days; PTU’s severe hepatitis (boxed warning) restricts it to the first trimester, thyroid storm, or methimazole reactions.
Both thionamides carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings; PTU has the greater liver risk. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop and check a CBC.
**●  Over-replacement:** tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.
Iodides given alone can escape in 2–8 weeks and worsen thyrotoxicosis; avoid chronic iodide in pregnancy (fetal goiter).
**Older adults and patients with cardiac disease: start at lower doses and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia.**
**●  Propranolol:** avoided in decompensated heart failure and asthma.
Radioactive iodine (131I) is avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding — it destroys the fetal thyroid.
**Significant absorption interactions: calcium, iron, and antacids can all reduce absorption — separate dosing by at least 4 hours.**
**●  Timing:** separate from calcium, iron, antacids, PPIs and bile acid binders by 4 hours.

Amiodarone and lithium can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism. Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise. Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine speed clearance of levothyroxine and steroids.
**●  Steroids:** also treat relative adrenal insufficiency; avoid aspirin in thyroid storm (it frees bound hormone).
Take on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, consistently relative to other medications and food.
T4 has a 7-day half-life (allows once-daily dosing); T3 about 1 day. Enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed thyroid hormone metabolism.
**●  Start low:** in older adults and in cardiac disease. Check TSH at 6–8 weeks.
The absorption-interaction list is extremely high-yield — many patients also take calcium or iron, so timing counseling matters as much as the drug itself.
The pregnancy-trimester switch (PTU in first trimester, methimazole after) is a frequently tested nuance — worth stating explicitly rather than assuming one drug is simply "better."
**●  Sequence:** start PTU and beta-blocker first; give iodine at least an hour later. **●  PTU:** boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.
Case: fever, tachycardia, and altered mental status in untreated Graves disease. **What is the correct sequence of pharmacologic therapy, and why does the order matter?**

**Beta-blockade and PTU are started first; iodine solution is given only after PTU, since giving iodine first would supply additional substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis before the gland’s synthetic machinery is blocked — potentially worsening the crisis.**
Iodine-first sequencing is the classic high-yield detail: giving iodine first can worsen the crisis by supplying substrate before synthesis is blocked.
Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal hormones) affects 4–10%; amiodarone causes hypo- or hyperthyroidism (about 3% thyrotoxicosis) that persists after stopping.
Subacute thyroiditis releases stored hormone transiently; nontoxic goiter in the US is most often Hashimoto thyroiditis; neonatal Graves comes from maternal antibodies.
Use · Methimazole: First-line for most non-pregnant patients; once daily · Propylthiouracil (PTU): First trimester of pregnancy; thyroid storm
Extra action · Methimazole: — · Propylthiouracil (PTU): Also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion
Pregnancy · Methimazole: Avoid in first trimester (teratogenic) · Propylthiouracil (PTU): Preferred in first trimester
Boxed warning · Methimazole: Agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity · Propylthiouracil (PTU): Severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole)

**Glucocorticoid power and mineralocorticoid balance — and what happens when therapy stops.**

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses CRH and ACTH via negative feedback, reducing endogenous cortisol production — abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.**
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — it explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.
Prednisone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone (glucocorticoids); fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid); ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone (antagonists).
Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone): anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, with a spectrum of relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity across agents.

Signaling (Figure 8): prednisone or cortisol crosses the cell membrane → binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex moves into the nucleus → switches on anti-inflammatory genes and represses NF-kB cytokines → fewer inflammatory cells and mediators.
Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Synthesis chain (Figure 10): cholesterol enters the adrenal cortex → CYP enzymes convert it to cortisol and aldosterone → ketoconazole blocks several enzymes; metyrapone blocks the last cortisol step (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Then cortisol or aldosterone binds its receptor → mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Receptor blockers leave hormone levels high.
Glucocorticoids are used across nearly every organ system for inflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Fludrocortisone: replacement therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), alongside a glucocorticoid — primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.
**●  Ketoconazole:** inhibits multiple steps in steroidogenesis (CYP enzymes); used for Cushing syndrome; significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity concerns.
**●  Metyrapone:** blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (11-β-hydroxylase); used diagnostically and for Cushing syndrome.

**●  Mifepristone:** a glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option (distinct from its progesterone-receptor antagonist use in pregnancy termination).

**●  Spironolactone:** a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperaldosteronism and as a potassium-sparing diuretic — ties back to the diuretic pharmacology concepts from earlier coursework.
Addison disease: hydrocortisone 20–30 mg daily (more during stress) plus fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/d.
Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing syndrome; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce neonatal respiratory distress.
**●  Adverse effects:** hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.
**●  Ketoconazole:** hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, strong CYP3A4 inhibition.
**●  Metyrapone:** raises androgens and deoxycorticosterone (hirsutism, hypertension).
**●  Mifepristone:** contraindicated in pregnancy; causes hypokalemia; cortisol levels rise, so monitor clinically. **●  Spironolactone:** hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
Adrenal suppression can occur after more than 2 weeks of corticosteroids; ACTH does not speed recovery.
Long-term steroids: Cushingoid changes, myopathy, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, masked infection, hypomania or psychosis, posterior subcapsular cataracts.
Azole antifungals raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium add to spironolactone hyperkalemia. Insulin and oral agents need adjusting during steroid therapy.
**●  Potency vs. hydrocortisone:** prednisone about 4x, dexamethasone about 25-30x. **●  Mineralocorticoid action:** fludrocortisone has it; hydrocortisone has both.
**●  Dosing:** take in the morning with food; consider bone and GI protection.
Synthetic corticosteroids — pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics: potency and salt-retaining activity differ by agent (equivalent-dose table).
Selection of drug & dosage schedule: give steroids as a single morning dose; alternate-day dosing lessens suppression when disease control allows.
Fludrocortisone: monitor blood pressure and potassium.
Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis; taper. Chronic suppression leaves the axis unable to resume adequate cortisol quickly — taper, don’t stop abruptly.

Case: chronic high-dose prednisone for a rheumatologic condition, stopped abruptly after running out of refills; now hypotension, weakness, nausea, confusion. **What is the most likely cause of this presentation, and how should it be managed?**
**This presentation is consistent with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal after HPA-axis suppression.**
**Management requires immediate IV hydrocortisone (which has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity) and IV fluids — this is a medical emergency, not a routine medication-refill issue.**
The fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill" — it is emergent IV steroid replacement; tapering protects against it.

Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly — don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Drug names reveal the class: **-tide** somatostatin analog (octreotide, lanreotide; lowers GH release); **-pressin** vasopressin analog (desmopressin; central diabetes insipidus); **-vaptan** V2 antagonist (tolvaptan; SIADH).

**-ergoline** dopamine agonist, ergot-derived (cabergoline; lowers prolactin); **-thyroxine** thyroid hormone (levothyroxine; replacement, titrate to TSH); **-imazole / -thiouracil** thionamide antithyroid (methimazole, propylthiouracil; blocks hormone synthesis).

**-sone / -solone** corticosteroid (prednisone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, taper); **-conazole** azole steroidogenesis inhibitor (ketoconazole; Cushing syndrome); **-pristone** receptor antagonist (mifepristone; glucocorticoid-receptor block); **-lactone** mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone; hyperkalemia risk).
**A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.**
Recap: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis (Figure 1) is a shared regulatory template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal systems — drug therapy can intervene at any level.

**2.** Thyroid hormone synthesis has distinct, drug-targetable steps (Figure 6); PTU uniquely blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it preferred in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy.
**3.** Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis (Figure 9) — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis, so chronic therapy is tapered, not stopped.

**4.** Adrenocortical antagonists (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone) block cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action at different points for Cushing syndrome and hyperaldosteronism. **5.** Session 2 (Thursday, November 12) continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders.
Older synthesis inhibitors — aminoglutethimide and trilostane — and the adrenolytic mitotane are rarely used; mifepristone (RU-486) is the receptor antagonist.
Synthesis inhibitors & glucocorticoid antagonists: metyrapone is the only adrenal inhibitor usable in pregnancy; abiraterone treats refractory prostate cancer; mifepristone half-life about 20 hours.

Monitor · Glucocorticoids (prednisone, dexamethasone): Glucose, bone, infection, mood; taper chronic use · Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): Blood pressure and potassium

1.title: Endocrine Pharmacotherapy
1.notes: Say: "One template runs this whole unit: hypothalamus drives the pituitary, the pituitary drives a target gland, and the gland's hormone feeds back to turn the levels above it down. Every drug today either replaces a hormone, blocks one, or interrupts that loop."

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes:
Orient students to the arc of this session: the shared HPA-template concept, then three organ systems in turn (pituitary, thyroid, adrenal) that all follow the same hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland logic introduced in Figure 1. Session 2 continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders on Nov 12.

Instructor script:

Objectives: Read them aloud.

3.notes:
Point students to the required and recommended texts for Unit 4 before diving into content. Katzung’s Chapters 37–42 are the required reading for this unit; Pharmacotherapy Principles and Practice is recommended as additional support, not a substitute. Session 1 covers Chapters 37–39; Session 2 covers Chapters 40–42.

Instructor script:

Readings: Katzung chapters 37-39 cover this session.

Section transition.

Section 01: the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, where every drug either replaces a hormone, blocks one, or interrupts the loop.

5.title: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Target Gland Axis
5.notes:
This is the conceptual spine for the entire unit — thyroid (Section 2), adrenal (Section 3), and gonadal (Session 2) pharmacology all map onto this same three-level axis. Keep returning to this diagram as each new system is introduced.

Instructor script:

Figure 1: Trace the axis and the negative-feedback arrows. Return to this figure every time we meet a new gland.

6.title: Growth Hormone Disorders
6.notes:
Acromegaly pharmacology is a good place to preview that octreotide will reappear later in GI/variceal contexts — reinforces that these drug classes are not siloed by organ system.

Instructor script:

Know: Somatropin treats GH deficiency; monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 in adults.

7.title: Somatostatin Analogs and Pegvisomant: Controlling GH Excess
7.notes:
Figure 2: Octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release. Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so IGF-1 falls.

Know: Monitor IGF-1 for acromegaly therapy. GH rises on pegvisomant and is not used to monitor it. Octreotide: gallstones, GI upset, bradycardia, glucose changes. Also used for carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.

8.title: Hyperprolactinemia and ADH Disorders
8.notes:
The DI vs. SIADH contrast is a classic exam pairing — anchor it to "which way does free water move" rather than memorizing drug names in isolation.

Instructor script:

Prolactin: dopamine is the brake on prolactin, shown on the next slide.

Ask: "Which way does free water move?" (ADH, covered on the following slides.)

9.title: Dopamine Agonists: Restoring the Brake on Prolactin
9.notes:
Figure 3: Dopamine is the brake on prolactin. Cabergoline and bromocriptine restore it and shrink prolactinomas.

Know: Cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated. High doses link to valvulopathy. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin.

10.title: ADH, Desmopressin and Tolvaptan: Which Way Does Water Move?
10.notes:
Figure 4: Desmopressin activates V2 receptors and keeps water. Tolvaptan and demeclocycline let water go.

Know: Desmopressin risks hyponatremia. Tolvaptan overcorrection risks osmotic demyelination, so start in hospital.

11.notes:
Section transition.

Section 02: thyroid and antithyroid drugs.

12.title: Levothyroxine for Hypothyroidism
12.notes:
The absorption-interaction list is extremely high-yield — many patients are also on calcium or iron supplements, so timing counseling matters as much as the drug itself.

Instructor script:

Know: About 1.6 mcg/kg/day is full replacement. Start low in older adults and cardiac disease. Check TSH at 6-8 weeks. Estrogen and pregnancy raise needs. Over-replacement causes atrial fibrillation and bone loss.

13.title: Levothyroxine: Absorption, Conversion and Timing
13.notes: Figure 5: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast, and separate calcium, iron and antacids by 4 hours.

14.title: Thyroid Hormone Synthesis: Where Antithyroid Drugs Act
14.notes:
This diagram is the mechanistic key to the next several slides — make sure students can explain why PTU, not methimazole, is preferred in thyroid storm using this figure alone (it blocks an extra step).

Instructor script:

Figure 6: Iodide trapping, organification, coupling and peripheral conversion. Methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling. PTU also blocks conversion.

15.title: Methimazole vs. Propylthiouracil (PTU)
15.notes:
The pregnancy-trimester switch (PTU in first trimester, methimazole after) is a frequently tested nuance — worth stating explicitly rather than letting students assume one drug is simply "better."

Instructor script:

Methimazole is first-line for most patients and is avoided in the first trimester. PTU is preferred in the first trimester and in storm.

Know: Both carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings; PTU has the greater liver risk. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop and check a CBC.

16.title: Thyroid Storm: A Multi-Drug Approach
16.notes:
The "iodine after PTU, not before" sequencing is a classic high-yield detail — giving iodine first can actually worsen the crisis by providing more substrate for hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked.

Instructor script:

Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets; the next two slides show the mechanism and the sequence.

17.title: Thyroid Storm: Four Drugs, Four Targets
17.notes: Figure 7: Four drugs, four targets: PTU blocks synthesis, iodine blocks release (after PTU), propranolol blunts symptoms, steroids blunt conversion.

18.title: Sequencing Therapy in Thyroid Storm
18.notes:
This case reinforces Figure 6 and the sequencing point from the prior slide — a good checkpoint for whether the mechanism actually landed, not just the drug names.

Instructor script:

Ask: "Why must iodine come after the thionamide?" Answer: iodine first provides substrate for new hormone.

20.title: Glucocorticoids vs. Mineralocorticoids
20.notes:
Fludrocortisone is often under-emphasized relative to glucocorticoids — make the point explicitly that primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.

Instructor script:

Know: Potency versus hydrocortisone: prednisone about 4x, dexamethasone about 25-30x. Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid action. Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid effect in Addison disease. Adverse effects: hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.

21.title: Glucocorticoid Receptor Signaling: How Steroids Quiet Inflammation
21.notes: Figure 8: The steroid binds the cytoplasmic receptor, enters the nucleus, and changes transcription; NF-kB driven cytokines are repressed.

22.title: Exogenous Corticosteroids and HPA Axis Suppression
22.notes:
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — every patient on chronic steroids is at risk of this, and it directly explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.

Instructor script:

Figure 9: Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH. Abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis; taper.

23.title: Adrenocortical Antagonists
23.notes:
Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly so students don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Instructor script:

Enzyme blockers (ketoconazole, metyrapone) lower cortisol.

Know: Ketoconazole: hepatotoxicity, QT, strong CYP3A4 inhibition. Metyrapone: androgen and deoxycorticosterone excess.

24.title: Blocking Steroid Synthesis vs. Blocking the Receptor
24.notes:
Figure 10: Receptor blockers (mifepristone, spironolactone) leave hormone levels high.

Know: Mifepristone: pregnancy contraindication, hypokalemia, misleading cortisol levels. Spironolactone: hyperkalemia.

This case is the direct clinical payoff of Figure 9 — emphasize that the fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill," it’s emergent IV steroid replacement.

Instructor script:

Missed refills with hypotension and confusion is adrenal crisis. Treat with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. Tapering protects against it.

30.title: Somatropin (Genotropin, Norditropin)
30.notes: Somatropin (Genotropin, Norditropin). Class: Recombinant human growth hormone. Formulation: SC injection pens and cartridges (several mg strengths). Dose (adult): Adults: start about 0.2 mg SC daily and titrate by IGF-1; children: weight-based daily SC dosing. Indications: GH deficiency (children and adults), Turner syndrome, other growth disorders. Adverse effects: Injection-site reaction, edema, joint pain, headache, hyperglycemia. Contraindications: Active malignancy, closed epiphyses (for growth promotion), acute critical illness. Toxicity / overdose: Fluid retention, glucose intolerance,

31.title: Octreotide (Sandostatin)
31.notes: Octreotide (Sandostatin). Class: Somatostatin analog. Formulation: SC injection 50/100/500 mcg/mL; LAR depot IM 10/20/30 mg; oral capsule. Dose (adult): Acromegaly: 50 mcg SC TID, titrate to 100-200 mcg TID; LAR 20 mg IM every 4 weeks. Indications: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma, esophageal variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: GI upset, diarrhea, gallstones, bradycardia, glucose changes. Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Gallstones, hypo- or hyperglycemia, bradycardia and conduction block; monitor IGF-1, glucose, gallbladder.

32.title: Lanreotide (Somatuline Depot)
32.notes: Lanreotide (Somatuline Depot). Class: Somatostatin analog. Formulation: Deep SC injection 60/90/120 mg prefilled syringe. Dose (adult): 90 mg deep SC every 4 weeks for 3 months, then adjust between 60 and 120 mg. Indications: Acromegaly, neuroendocrine tumors, carcinoid syndrome. Adverse effects: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, gallstones, injection-site reaction, bradycardia. Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Gallstones, glucose dysregulation, bradycardia; monitor GH and IGF-1.

33.title: Pegvisomant (Somavert)
33.notes: Pegvisomant (Somavert). Class: GH receptor antagonist. Formulation: SC injection vials 10/15/20/25/30 mg. Dose (adult): Load 40 mg SC, then 10 mg SC daily, titrate by IGF-1 (max 30 mg/day). Indications: Acromegaly not controlled by surgery or somatostatin analogs. Adverse effects: Injection-site reaction, headache, raised liver enzymes, flu-like symptoms. Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Liver injury; monitor tumor size by MRI; GH levels rise and are not used for monitoring.

34.title: Cabergoline (Dostinex)
34.notes: Cabergoline (Dostinex). Class: Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived). Formulation: Tablet 0.5 mg. Dose (adult): 0.25 mg PO twice weekly, increase by 0.25 mg every 4 weeks to usual max 1 mg twice weekly. Indications: Hyperprolactinemia, prolactinoma. Adverse effects: Nausea, dizziness, headache, orthostatic hypotension. Contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, cardiac valvulopathy, ergot hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Cardiac valve fibrosis at high doses; impulse-control and psychiatric effects; overdose causes hypotension and nausea.

35.title: Bromocriptine (Parlodel, Cycloset)
35.notes: Bromocriptine (Parlodel, Cycloset). Class: Dopamine D2 agonist (ergot-derived). Formulation: Tablet 2.5 mg; capsule 5 mg; Cycloset 0.8 mg tablet. Dose (adult): 1.25-2.5 mg PO at bedtime, titrate to 2.5 mg BID-TID for prolactinoma (max 15 mg/day). Indications: Hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly (adjunct), Parkinson disease, type 2 diabetes (Cycloset). Adverse effects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, headache, nasal congestion. Contraindications: Uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy-related hypertension, ergot hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Hypotension and syncope, psychosis, fib

36.title: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
36.notes: Desmopressin (DDAVP). Class: Synthetic vasopressin V2 agonist. Formulation: Tablet 0.1/0.2 mg; nasal spray; SC/IV 4 mcg/mL; ODT 60 mcg. Dose (adult): Central DI: 0.05-0.2 mg PO BID, or 10-40 mcg intranasal daily in divided doses; titrate to urine output. Indications: Central diabetes insipidus, nocturnal enuresis, hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (IV). Adverse effects: Headache, nausea, flushing, hyponatremia. Contraindications: Hyponatremia history, polydipsia, eGFR below 50, heart failure. Toxicity / overdose: Water intoxication with severe hyponatremia and seizures; limit fluids and

37.title: Tolvaptan (Samsca)
37.notes: Tolvaptan (Samsca). Class: Vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist. Formulation: Tablet 15/30 mg. Dose (adult): 15 mg PO once daily, titrate to 30-60 mg; start in hospital. Indications: Hyponatremia from SIADH or heart failure. Adverse effects: Thirst, dry mouth, polyuria, hypernatremia, liver injury. Contraindications: Urgent need to raise sodium, hypovolemia, anuria, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors. Toxicity / overdose: Overly rapid sodium correction (osmotic demyelination); liver injury; limit therapy to 30 days.

38.title: Demeclocycline
38.notes: Demeclocycline. Class: Tetracycline with ADH-antagonist effect. Formulation: Tablet 150/300 mg. Dose (adult): 150-300 mg PO 3-4 times daily for SIADH (off-label). Indications: Refractory SIADH (off-label), bacterial infections. Adverse effects: Photosensitivity, nausea, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Contraindications: Pregnancy, children under 8 years, hypersensitivity, severe renal impairment. Toxicity / overdose: Nephrotoxicity, photosensitivity, tooth discoloration; separate from calcium and antacids.

39.title: Levothyroxine (Synthroid, Levoxyl)
39.notes: Levothyroxine (Synthroid, Levoxyl). Class: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4). Formulation: Tablet 25-300 mcg (12 strengths); IV 100-500 mcg vial; liquid and capsule. Dose (adult): Full replacement about 1.6 mcg/kg/day PO; start 12.5-50 mcg in older adults or heart disease; recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks. Indications: Hypothyroidism, myxedema coma (IV), TSH suppression in thyroid cancer. Adverse effects: Usually none at the right dose; over-replacement causes tachycardia, tremor, insomnia, bone loss. Contraindications: Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency, acute MI, hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: O

40.title: Methimazole (Tapazole)
40.notes: Methimazole (Tapazole). Class: Thionamide antithyroid drug. Formulation: Tablet 5/10 mg. Dose (adult): Graves disease: start 10-30 mg PO once daily; adjust to free T4 every 4-6 weeks. Indications: Graves disease, toxic nodular goiter, pre-operative control. Adverse effects: Rash, itching, joint pain, taste change; agranulocytosis (rare). Contraindications: First trimester of pregnancy; prior methimazole agranulocytosis. Toxicity / overdose: Agranulocytosis (fever or sore throat: stop and check CBC), hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity.

41.title: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
41.notes: Propylthiouracil (PTU). Class: Thionamide antithyroid drug (also blocks T4 to T3). Formulation: Tablet 50 mg. Dose (adult): Start 100 mg PO TID (up to 300-400 mg/day); thyroid storm: 500-1,000 mg load, then 250 mg every 4 hours. Indications: First-trimester Graves disease, thyroid storm, methimazole intolerance. Adverse effects: Rash, nausea, taste change, joint pain. Contraindications: Prior PTU liver injury; avoid in children. Toxicity / overdose: Boxed warning: severe liver failure; agranulocytosis; ANCA-positive vasculitis.

42.title: Propranolol (Inderal)
42.notes: Propranolol (Inderal). Class: Nonselective beta-blocker. Formulation: Tablet 10/20/40/60/80 mg; ER capsule; IV 1 mg/mL. Dose (adult): Thyrotoxic symptoms: 20-40 mg PO every 6-8 hours; thyroid storm: 60-80 mg PO every 4 hours or 0.5-1 mg IV. Indications: Thyrotoxic symptoms, thyroid storm, hypertension, tremor. Adverse effects: Bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm, masks hypoglycemia. Contraindications: Asthma, decompensated heart failure, high-grade AV block, severe bradycardia. Toxicity / overdose: Bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm; avoid abrupt stopping; may mask hypoglycemia.

43.title: Potassium iodide (SSKI, Lugol solution)
43.notes: Potassium iodide (SSKI, Lugol solution). Class: Iodine (blocks hormone release). Formulation: SSKI 1 g/mL solution; Lugol 5% solution; tablets 65/130 mg. Dose (adult): Thyroid storm: 5 drops (about 250 mg) SSKI PO every 6 hours, at least 1 hour after a thionamide. Indications: Thyroid storm, pre-thyroidectomy preparation, radiation protection. Adverse effects: Metallic taste, GI upset, salivary gland swelling, rash. Contraindications: Giving before a thionamide; iodine allergy. Toxicity / overdose: Iodism (rash, swelling, fever); thyroid escape after about 10 days; hypo- or hyperthyroidism.

44.title: Prednisone
44.notes: Prednisone. Class: Glucocorticoid (prodrug of prednisolone). Formulation: Tablet 1/2.5/5/10/20/50 mg; oral solution. Dose (adult): 5-60 mg PO daily depending on indication; taper after more than 3 weeks of therapy. Indications: Inflammatory and autoimmune disease, allergic reactions. Adverse effects: Hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood change, weight gain, infection, osteoporosis. Contraindications: Systemic fungal infection; live vaccines at high dose. Toxicity / overdose: Adrenal suppression and crisis on abrupt stopping; Cushingoid features, cataracts, avascular necrosis.

45.title: Dexamethasone (Decadron)
45.notes: Dexamethasone (Decadron). Class: Long-acting glucocorticoid. Formulation: Tablet 0.5-6 mg; oral solution; IV 4/10 mg/mL. Dose (adult): 0.5-9 mg PO or IV daily by indication; cerebral edema 10 mg IV load, then 4 mg every 6 hours; thyroid storm 2 mg IV every 6 hours. Indications: Cerebral edema, antiemetic, severe inflammation, Cushing screening test. Adverse effects: Insomnia, hyperglycemia, mood change, immune suppression. Contraindications: Systemic fungal infection, hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Potency about 25-30 times hydrocortisone with no mineralocorticoid effect; adrenal suppr

46.title: Hydrocortisone (Cortef, Solu-Cortef)
46.notes: Hydrocortisone (Cortef, Solu-Cortef). Class: Glucocorticoid with mineralocorticoid activity. Formulation: Tablet 5/10/20 mg; IV 100 mg vial. Dose (adult): Replacement 15-25 mg/day PO in 2-3 divided doses; adrenal crisis 100 mg IV, then 200 mg over 24 hours. Indications: Adrenal insufficiency, adrenal crisis, inflammatory conditions. Adverse effects: Hyperglycemia, fluid retention, mood change, infection risk. Contraindications: Systemic fungal infection. Toxicity / overdose: Excess causes Cushingoid features, hypertension, hypokalemia; stress-dose during illness and surgery.

47.title: Fludrocortisone (Florinef)
47.notes: Fludrocortisone (Florinef). Class: Mineralocorticoid. Formulation: Tablet 0.1 mg. Dose (adult): 0.05-0.2 mg PO once daily. Indications: Primary adrenal insufficiency (with a glucocorticoid), orthostatic hypotension. Adverse effects: Hypertension, edema, hypokalemia, headache. Contraindications: Systemic fungal infection; caution in heart failure. Toxicity / overdose: Hypokalemia, fluid overload, supine hypertension; monitor blood pressure and potassium.

48.title: Ketoconazole
48.notes: Ketoconazole. Class: Azole antifungal and steroidogenesis inhibitor. Formulation: Tablet 200 mg. Dose (adult): Cushing syndrome (off-label): start 200 mg PO BID, usual 400-1,200 mg/day divided. Indications: Cushing syndrome (off-label), fungal infections. Adverse effects: Nausea, abdominal pain, headache, gynecomastia, adrenal insufficiency. Contraindications: Liver disease, QT prolongation or interacting QT drugs, pregnancy. Toxicity / overdose: Boxed hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation; strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; monitor LFTs and ECG.

49.title: Metyrapone (Metopirone)
49.notes: Metyrapone (Metopirone). Class: 11-beta-hydroxylase inhibitor. Formulation: Capsule 250 mg. Dose (adult): Cushing syndrome: start 250 mg PO TID-QID, titrate to cortisol (up to 6 g/day); diagnostic test: 30 mg/kg once at midnight. Indications: Cushing syndrome, diagnostic test of the HPA axis. Adverse effects: Nausea, dizziness, hypertension, edema, hirsutism. Contraindications: Adrenal insufficiency, hypersensitivity. Toxicity / overdose: Adrenal insufficiency, hypokalemia, hypertension from deoxycorticosterone, androgen excess.

50.title: Mifepristone (Korlym)
50.notes: Mifepristone (Korlym). Class: Glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist. Formulation: Tablet 300 mg (Cushing); 200 mg (pregnancy termination). Dose (adult): Cushing hyperglycemia: 300 mg PO daily with a meal, titrate up to 1,200 mg/day. Indications: Hyperglycemia with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option. Adverse effects: Fatigue, nausea, headache, hypokalemia, edema, endometrial thickening. Contraindications: Pregnancy (boxed warning), simvastatin or lovastatin, need for long-term corticosteroids. Toxicity / overdose: Pregnancy loss; adrenal insufficiency (cortisol rises so labs mislead);

51.title: Spironolactone (Aldactone)
51.notes: Spironolactone (Aldactone). Class: Mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist. Formulation: Tablet 25/50/100 mg. Dose (adult): Hyperaldosteronism: 25-100 mg PO daily (up to 400 mg); heart failure 12.5-50 mg daily. Indications: Primary hyperaldosteronism, heart failure, resistant hypertension, edema, hirsutism (off-label). Adverse effects: Hyperkalemia, gynecomastia, menstrual irregularity, dizziness. Contraindications: Hyperkalemia, Addison disease, severe renal impairment. Toxicity / overdose: Life-threatening hyperkalemia (with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium); monitor potassium and creatinine.

U4-R1.question: Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis template: what does the peripheral hormone do to the levels above it, and why does that matter for every exogenous hormone therapy in this unit?
U4-R1.answer: The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — this explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit (glucocorticoids, combined contraception) suppresses its corresponding axis.

U4-R2.question: Compare the drug strategies for GH deficiency vs. GH excess (acromegaly), naming at least one agent for each.

U4-R3.question: Why are dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) first-line for hyperprolactinemia?
U4-R3.answer: Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin; agonists restore that inhibitory tone.

U4-R4.question: Contrast diabetes insipidus and SIADH: which direction does each move free water, and what is the first-line drug strategy for each?

U4-R5.question: What is levothyroxine's narrow-therapeutic-index monitoring parameter, and what three substances significantly reduce its absorption if taken too close together?
U4-R5.answer: TSH; calcium, iron, antacids (separate by ≥4 hours).

U4-R6.question: Compare methimazole and PTU: which is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm, and why?

U4-R7.question: In thyroid storm, why must iodine solution be given only after PTU or methimazole, not before?
U4-R7.answer: Giving iodine first would supply substrate for new hormone synthesis before synthesis is blocked, worsening the crisis.

U4-R8.question: Explain why abruptly stopping chronic high-dose glucocorticoid therapy can precipitate adrenal insufficiency. What is the correct approach instead?
U4-R8.answer: Chronic suppression of CRH/ACTH leaves the axis unable to resume adequate cortisol quickly — taper, don't stop abruptly.

U4-R9.question: Name one adrenocortical antagonist and the specific step of cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action it blocks.
U4-R9.answer: E.g., ketoconazole (steroidogenic CYP enzymes), metyrapone (11-β-hydroxylase), mifepristone (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist), spironolactone (mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist).

children.name: Class
facts: **One regulatory template governs thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal control alike.**

**Figure 1. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the hypothalamus drives the anterior pituitary, which drives a target endocrine gland, whose peripheral hormone produces end-organ effects and negatively feeds back to suppress the levels above it.**
This is the conceptual spine for the unit — thyroid, adrenal and gonadal pharmacology all map onto this three-level axis; return to it every time a new gland appears.
The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — which explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit suppresses the levels above it.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Somatropin (GH deficiency); octreotide, lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH excess); cabergoline, bromocriptine (prolactin); desmopressin (DI); tolvaptan, demeclocycline (SIADH).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: GH axis (Figure 2): pituitary somatotroph releases GH → GH drives liver IGF-1 production → octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release.
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls → acromegaly symptoms improve (monitor IGF-1). GH rises on pegvisomant, so GH is not used to monitor it.

Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release — dopamine agonists restore that inhibitory tone. Hypothalamic dopamine is the brake on lactotrophs; prolactinoma or drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) lift the brake.
Cabergoline or bromocriptine activate D2 receptors → prolactin release falls and the tumor often shrinks → cycles and fertility return; galactorrhea resolves.
ADH (Figure 4): ADH binds the V2 receptor in the collecting duct → aquaporin-2 channels insert → water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
Desmopressin boosts this (diabetes insipidus); tolvaptan or demeclocycline blunt it (SIADH) → free water retained in DI therapy, excreted in SIADH therapy.
Anterior pituitary hormones & their hypothalamic regulators: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs down-regulate GnRH receptors and suppress LH and FSH.

children.name: Indications
facts: **●  GH deficiency:** treated with recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin); monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 levels in adults.

**●  GH excess (acromegaly):** treated with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide — suppress GH release), the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or dopamine agonists (cabergoline) in select cases.
**●  Clinical pearl:** octreotide also has major uses outside the pituitary axis — variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome — worth flagging as a cross-system agent.
**●  Indication:** octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly; octreotide also treats carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.
Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine agonists are first-line — cabergoline, bromocriptine — used for prolactinomas and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency/resistance): desmopressin (DDAVP) for central DI. SIADH (ADH excess): fluid restriction first-line; vasopressin-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline for refractory cases.
**●  Somatropin (GH deficiency):** monitor growth velocity or IGF-1.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **●  Adverse effects:** GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia with octreotide and lanreotide (also glucose changes).
**●  Limitation:** pegvisomant does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.
**●  Adverse effects:** nausea, orthostatic hypotension and dizziness (dopamine agonists).
Cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated; high doses link to valvulopathy.
**●  Caution:** high-dose cabergoline in Parkinson patients is linked to cardiac valve fibrosis; use caution with severe psychiatric disease and avoid unmonitored antipsychotic changes.
**●  Desmopressin:** risk is hyponatremia; monitor sodium and limit fluids.
**●  Tolvaptan:** can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and cause liver injury; start in hospital.
**●  SIADH:** first-line is fluid restriction; demeclocycline causes photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity.
Short stature from GH deficiency, Turner syndrome and other growth disorders is the main somatropin use; long-acting weekly forms (somapacitan) exist.
Growth hormone (somatropin) adverse effects are rare: pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression, edema, hyperglycemia.
Mecasermin (recombinant IGF-I for GH-unresponsive growth failure) causes hypoglycemia — give with a carbohydrate meal within 20 minutes.
Octreotide: nausea, cramps, steatorrhea, gallstones, and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin by blocking dopamine.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **●  Dosing:** cabergoline is better tolerated and given twice weekly; bromocriptine is daily.
Octreotide is 45 times more potent than somatostatin at inhibiting GH; somatostatin analogs come as long-acting monthly depots. Cabergoline’s half-life is about 65 hours.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **●  Monitoring:** pregnancy testing and prolactin monitoring (dopamine agonists). Monitor IGF-1 for acromegaly therapy.
Pegvisomant does not lower GH secretion and may let the adenoma grow — monitor IGF-I and yearly pituitary MRI.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: DI vs. SIADH is a classic exam pairing — opposite problems; anchor it to "which way does free water move" rather than drug names in isolation.
Octreotide reappears in GI/variceal contexts — drug classes are not siloed by organ system.
Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism — infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in women; low libido and ED in men; macroadenomas can compress the optic nerves.
Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is given IV to start or augment labor; it also triggers milk letdown. Its half-life is about 5 minutes.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Levothyroxine (replacement); methimazole, propylthiouracil (thionamides); propranolol; potassium iodide.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3.**
Levothyroxine path (Figure 5): tablet taken on an empty stomach → absorbed in the small intestine; calcium, iron and antacid binders block it.
T4 converted to active T3 in tissues → T3 binds nuclear receptors and restores metabolism → TSH falls to the target range (recheck at 6–8 weeks).
Methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling; PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion — a faster symptomatic effect in crisis.
Storm targets (Figure 7): Graves thyroid makes excess hormone — PTU blocks synthesis; hormone is released — iodine (after PTU) blocks release.

T4 converts to T3 in tissues — PTU, propranolol and steroids block conversion; T3 stimulates beta receptors — propranolol blunts tachycardia and tremor; crisis settles with fluids, cooling and support.
Thyroid physiology: large doses of iodine inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff block); amiodarone, contrast, β blockers and corticosteroids inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion.

children.name: Indications
facts: Levothyroxine: first-line for hypothyroidism; narrow therapeutic index — dose titrated using TSH (primary hypothyroidism) with repeat labs every 6–8 weeks after a dose change.
About 1.6 mcg/kg/day is full replacement; estrogen raises needs. **●  Pregnancy:** often raises dose needs; monitor TSH closely.
Methimazole: first-line for most non-pregnant patients — once-daily dosing, more convenient; avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
PTU: preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm. PTU first trimester (lower teratogenic risk) and thyroid storm (also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).
**A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.** Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets.

Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. PTU (preferred over methimazole) — blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.

Iodine solution (given after PTU/methimazole) — acutely blocks hormone release; must follow the antithyroid drug to avoid providing substrate for new synthesis. Corticosteroids — blunt peripheral conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

Laboratory diagnosis of Graves disease: suppressed TSH with high free thyroid hormone. Management of Graves disease: antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy; methimazole preferred except in pregnancy and storm.
Pregnant hypothyroid patients often need about 25–30% more levothyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: Methimazole boxed warning: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. PTU boxed warning: severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole) — reserve for specific indications.
Thioamide agranulocytosis occurs in 0.1–0.5%, usually within the first 90 days; PTU’s severe hepatitis (boxed warning) restricts it to the first trimester, thyroid storm, or methimazole reactions.
Both thionamides carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings; PTU has the greater liver risk. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop and check a CBC.
**●  Over-replacement:** tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.
Iodides given alone can escape in 2–8 weeks and worsen thyrotoxicosis; avoid chronic iodide in pregnancy (fetal goiter).

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Older adults and patients with cardiac disease: start at lower doses and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia.**
**●  Propranolol:** avoided in decompensated heart failure and asthma.
Radioactive iodine (131I) is avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding — it destroys the fetal thyroid.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Significant absorption interactions: calcium, iron, and antacids can all reduce absorption — separate dosing by at least 4 hours.**
**●  Timing:** separate from calcium, iron, antacids, PPIs and bile acid binders by 4 hours.

Amiodarone and lithium can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism. Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise. Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine speed clearance of levothyroxine and steroids.
**●  Steroids:** also treat relative adrenal insufficiency; avoid aspirin in thyroid storm (it frees bound hormone).

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Take on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, consistently relative to other medications and food.
T4 has a 7-day half-life (allows once-daily dosing); T3 about 1 day. Enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed thyroid hormone metabolism.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **●  Start low:** in older adults and in cardiac disease. Check TSH at 6–8 weeks.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The absorption-interaction list is extremely high-yield — many patients also take calcium or iron, so timing counseling matters as much as the drug itself.
The pregnancy-trimester switch (PTU in first trimester, methimazole after) is a frequently tested nuance — worth stating explicitly rather than assuming one drug is simply "better."
**●  Sequence:** start PTU and beta-blocker first; give iodine at least an hour later. **●  PTU:** boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.
Case: fever, tachycardia, and altered mental status in untreated Graves disease. **What is the correct sequence of pharmacologic therapy, and why does the order matter?**

**Beta-blockade and PTU are started first; iodine solution is given only after PTU, since giving iodine first would supply additional substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis before the gland’s synthetic machinery is blocked — potentially worsening the crisis.**
Iodine-first sequencing is the classic high-yield detail: giving iodine first can worsen the crisis by supplying substrate before synthesis is blocked.
Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal hormones) affects 4–10%; amiodarone causes hypo- or hyperthyroidism (about 3% thyrotoxicosis) that persists after stopping.
Subacute thyroiditis releases stored hormone transiently; nontoxic goiter in the US is most often Hashimoto thyroiditis; neonatal Graves comes from maternal antibodies.

children.name: Class
facts: **Glucocorticoid power and mineralocorticoid balance — and what happens when therapy stops.**

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses CRH and ACTH via negative feedback, reducing endogenous cortisol production — abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.**
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — it explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Prednisone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone (glucocorticoids); fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid); ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone (antagonists).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone): anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, with a spectrum of relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity across agents.

Signaling (Figure 8): prednisone or cortisol crosses the cell membrane → binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex moves into the nucleus → switches on anti-inflammatory genes and represses NF-kB cytokines → fewer inflammatory cells and mediators.
Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Synthesis chain (Figure 10): cholesterol enters the adrenal cortex → CYP enzymes convert it to cortisol and aldosterone → ketoconazole blocks several enzymes; metyrapone blocks the last cortisol step (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Then cortisol or aldosterone binds its receptor → mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Receptor blockers leave hormone levels high.

children.name: Indications
facts: Glucocorticoids are used across nearly every organ system for inflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Fludrocortisone: replacement therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), alongside a glucocorticoid — primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.
**●  Ketoconazole:** inhibits multiple steps in steroidogenesis (CYP enzymes); used for Cushing syndrome; significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity concerns.
**●  Metyrapone:** blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (11-β-hydroxylase); used diagnostically and for Cushing syndrome.

**●  Mifepristone:** a glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option (distinct from its progesterone-receptor antagonist use in pregnancy termination).

**●  Spironolactone:** a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperaldosteronism and as a potassium-sparing diuretic — ties back to the diuretic pharmacology concepts from earlier coursework.
Addison disease: hydrocortisone 20–30 mg daily (more during stress) plus fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/d.
Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing syndrome; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce neonatal respiratory distress.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **●  Adverse effects:** hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.
**●  Ketoconazole:** hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, strong CYP3A4 inhibition.
**●  Metyrapone:** raises androgens and deoxycorticosterone (hirsutism, hypertension).
**●  Mifepristone:** contraindicated in pregnancy; causes hypokalemia; cortisol levels rise, so monitor clinically. **●  Spironolactone:** hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
Adrenal suppression can occur after more than 2 weeks of corticosteroids; ACTH does not speed recovery.
Long-term steroids: Cushingoid changes, myopathy, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, masked infection, hypomania or psychosis, posterior subcapsular cataracts.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Azole antifungals raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium add to spironolactone hyperkalemia. Insulin and oral agents need adjusting during steroid therapy.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: **●  Potency vs. hydrocortisone:** prednisone about 4x, dexamethasone about 25-30x. **●  Mineralocorticoid action:** fludrocortisone has it; hydrocortisone has both.
**●  Dosing:** take in the morning with food; consider bone and GI protection.
Synthetic corticosteroids — pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics: potency and salt-retaining activity differ by agent (equivalent-dose table).
Selection of drug & dosage schedule: give steroids as a single morning dose; alternate-day dosing lessens suppression when disease control allows.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Fludrocortisone: monitor blood pressure and potassium.
Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis; taper. Chronic suppression leaves the axis unable to resume adequate cortisol quickly — taper, don’t stop abruptly.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: chronic high-dose prednisone for a rheumatologic condition, stopped abruptly after running out of refills; now hypotension, weakness, nausea, confusion. **What is the most likely cause of this presentation, and how should it be managed?**
**This presentation is consistent with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal after HPA-axis suppression.**
**Management requires immediate IV hydrocortisone (which has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity) and IV fluids — this is a medical emergency, not a routine medication-refill issue.**
The fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill" — it is emergent IV steroid replacement; tapering protects against it.

Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly — don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Drug names reveal the class: **-tide** somatostatin analog (octreotide, lanreotide; lowers GH release); **-pressin** vasopressin analog (desmopressin; central diabetes insipidus); **-vaptan** V2 antagonist (tolvaptan; SIADH).

**-ergoline** dopamine agonist, ergot-derived (cabergoline; lowers prolactin); **-thyroxine** thyroid hormone (levothyroxine; replacement, titrate to TSH); **-imazole / -thiouracil** thionamide antithyroid (methimazole, propylthiouracil; blocks hormone synthesis).

**-sone / -solone** corticosteroid (prednisone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, taper); **-conazole** azole steroidogenesis inhibitor (ketoconazole; Cushing syndrome); **-pristone** receptor antagonist (mifepristone; glucocorticoid-receptor block); **-lactone** mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone; hyperkalemia risk).
**A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.**
Recap: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis (Figure 1) is a shared regulatory template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal systems — drug therapy can intervene at any level.

**2.** Thyroid hormone synthesis has distinct, drug-targetable steps (Figure 6); PTU uniquely blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it preferred in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy.
**3.** Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis (Figure 9) — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis, so chronic therapy is tapered, not stopped.

**4.** Adrenocortical antagonists (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone) block cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action at different points for Cushing syndrome and hyperaldosteronism. **5.** Session 2 (Thursday, November 12) continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders.
Older synthesis inhibitors — aminoglutethimide and trilostane — and the adrenolytic mitotane are rarely used; mifepristone (RU-486) is the receptor antagonist.
Synthesis inhibitors & glucocorticoid antagonists: metyrapone is the only adrenal inhibitor usable in pregnancy; abiraterone treats refractory prostate cancer; mifepristone half-life about 20 hours.

hy: Acromegaly: octreotide/lanreotide or pegvisomant (monitor IGF-1); prolactinoma: cabergoline; DI: desmopressin (hyponatremia); SIADH: fluid restriction, then tolvaptan.
Levothyroxine: empty stomach, separate calcium/iron/antacids by 4 h, TSH at 6–8 weeks, start low in older/cardiac patients.
PTU for storm and first trimester; methimazole otherwise; fever/sore throat → stop, CBC.
Chronic steroids suppress CRH/ACTH → taper; abrupt stop → adrenal crisis → IV hydrocortisone + fluids.
Addison disease needs a glucocorticoid plus fludrocortisone.
